lesson.title: A Flat Spot Guaranteed: Rolle's Theorem
lesson.summary: When a function starts and ends at the same height, the Mean Value Theorem's average rate of change is automatically zero, which means the guaranteed point c must have a perfectly horizontal tangent line. This special case is important enough to have its own name: Rolle's Theorem.
lesson.body:
Look again at the Mean Value Theorem's conclusion, f'(c) = [f(b)-f(a)] / (b-a), and consider what happens in the special situation where f(a) equals f(b). The numerator on the right, f(b) - f(a), becomes 0, so the whole average rate of change collapses to 0, regardless of how far apart a and b are. Plugging that into the conclusion, the Mean Value Theorem now guarantees a point c in (a,b) with f'(c) = 0, meaning the tangent line at c is perfectly horizontal. That special case, function values equal at both ends, guaranteed horizontal tangent somewhere in between, is Rolle's Theorem. It is not a separate theorem requiring new machinery; it is exactly what the Mean Value Theorem says when the secant line connecting the endpoints happens to be horizontal.

Formally, Rolle's Theorem states: if f is continuous on [a,b], differentiable on (a,b), and f(a) = f(b), then there exists at least one c in (a,b) with f'(c) = 0. Every function satisfying Rolle's Theorem's hypotheses also satisfies the Mean Value Theorem's hypotheses, since the extra condition f(a) = f(b) is added on top, not swapped in for continuity or differentiability.

Try f(x) = x^2 - 4x + 3 on the interval [1,3]. Check the equal endpoints condition first: f(1) = 1 - 4 + 3 = 0, and f(3) = 9 - 12 + 3 = 0, so f(1) = f(3) = 0, satisfying Rolle's extra hypothesis. As a polynomial, f is continuous and differentiable everywhere, so all three conditions hold on [1,3]. Rolle's Theorem guarantees a c in (1,3) with f'(c) = 0. Since f'(x) = 2x - 4, setting 2c - 4 = 0 gives c = 2, which does lie in the open interval (1,3). Checking, f'(2) = 2(2) - 4 = 0, exactly as promised. There is a nice way to see why this had to happen: f(x) factors as (x-1)(x-3), a parabola with roots at x=1 and x=3 and a vertex exactly halfway between them, at x = 2, where the parabola bottoms out and its tangent is horizontal. Rolle's Theorem is really guaranteeing that same kind of turning point for any function with equal endpoint values, not just parabolas.

The horizontal tangent conclusion of Rolle's Theorem is also the seed of a broader idea used constantly in later calculus: between any two points where a function has the same value, there must be at least one critical point in between. That single observation underlies why a smooth function cannot cross the same height twice without pausing, even momentarily, somewhere in between.
